title: Numerical solution of equations
overview: Apply iterative methods to harder equations, justifying convergence and the accuracy of your final answer. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.
syllabusPoints: Locate roots using graphs or a sign change.
Relate xₙ₊₁=F(xₙ) to the equation being solved.
Carry out iterations accurately and recognise possible failure to converge.
Justify a root to a prescribed degree of accuracy.

definitions.definition: A value α for which f(α)=0.
Repeatedly applying xₙ₊₁=F(xₙ) to generate approximations.
The approximations approach a fixed limiting value.
f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs, guaranteeing at least one root in (a,b) when f is continuous.

sections.title: Locating a root
content: For continuous f, calculate f(a) and f(b). If f(a)f(b)<0, at least one root lies between a and b. A graph helps choose a sensible interval, but a sign change alone does not prove uniqueness.
bullets: State continuity when giving a formal sign-change justification.
An even-multiplicity root may touch the axis without changing sign.

examples.label: Key relationship
examples.content: Sign-change test: f(a)f(b)<0 ⇒ at least one root in (a,b), if f is continuous

sections.title: Building an iteration
content: Rearrange f(x)=0 into x=F(x), then use xₙ₊₁=F(xₙ). Different rearrangements can converge, oscillate or diverge. Use the starting value given and retain calculator precision through the table.
bullets: Show enough consecutive values for the examiner to follow the process.
Do not replace F(xₙ) with f(xₙ).

sections.title: Understanding convergence
content: A convergent sequence settles near a fixed point α where α=F(α). Cobweb thinking explains why some iterations move toward the intersection y=F(x), y=x and others move away; the syllabus expects recognition of failure even if the derivative test is not required.
bullets: Oscillation may still converge if its size shrinks.
A calculator error message can indicate the rearrangement leaves its valid domain.

sections.title: Proving the stated accuracy
content: A rounded decimal needs a bracket around the true root. For a value r correct to k decimal places, test the half-unit boundaries r±0.5×10⁻ᵏ and show f changes sign there, assuming continuity and a single relevant root.
bullets: Repeated equal displayed iterates suggest accuracy but do not by themselves prove it.
Use unrounded boundaries and function values.

formulas.label: Sign-change test
formulas.expression: f(a)f(b)<0 ⇒ at least one root in (a,b), if f is continuous

diagram.title: Numerical solution of equations: revision route

examTips: Keep full calculator precision during iteration and round only the requested final value.
Write f(a) and f(b) with their signs, not only the product.
Show the mathematical setup and exact working before the final rounded answer; unsupported calculator output may not earn method marks.
commonMistakes: Claiming a sign change proves there is exactly one root.
Using rounded iterates inside later iterations.
Proving accuracy with endpoints that do not match the requested rounding interval.

quickRecall.question: What must accompany a sign change to guarantee a root?
quickRecall.answer: Continuity of f on the interval.

quickRecall.question: What equation does the limit of xₙ₊₁=F(xₙ) satisfy?
How do you justify a root to 3 decimal places?
quickRecall.answer: Show a sign change at the two rounding boundaries r±0.0005, with the relevant continuity/uniqueness context.

quickRecall.question: Can a root exist without a sign change?
quickRecall.answer: Yes; an even-multiplicity root can touch the axis and turn back.
